title: Light constraints leave a scale to determine
question: What map can respect both light directions?
recap: Ask for a linear map that keeps light at speed c in both directions along the motion, and space and time must mix. One overall factor is left over; going there and back, and the symmetry of space, fix it at gamma.
premises: The two frames’ axes are parallel, and their origins coincide at time zero.
Space and time are the same everywhere, so the map between coordinates is linear.
The two postulates hold, together with going there and back, the symmetry of space, and continuity at zero speed.
limitations: Keeping one light ray at speed c does not fix every coefficient of the map.
The spacetime interval and matrices check the result later; the 1905 argument does not assume them.

overview.text: Ask for a linear map that keeps light at speed \(c\) in both directions along the motion, and space and time must mix. One overall factor is left over; going there and back, and the symmetry of space, fix it at \(\gamma\).

full.text: The moving origin follows \(x = vt\), so write \(x' = a(v)(x - vt)\). Requiring \(x' = ct'\) on \(x = ct\) and \(x' = -ct'\) on \(x = -ct\) fixes the time combination: \(t' = a(v)(t - vx/c^2)\). An overall scale \(a(v)\) remains.

full.spoken: The light constraints give a common coefficient multiplying x minus vt and t minus vx over c squared.

full.text: Going to the moving frame and back, with speed \(v\) and then \(-v\), must return every event unchanged, which gives \(a(v)\,a(-v)\,(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1\). Space has no preferred direction, so \(a(v) = a(-v)\), and since \(a(0) = 1\) the positive root is the one: \(a(v) = \gamma\).

full.spoken: The Lorentz factor is one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, giving the standard space and time transformation.

full.returnCaption: Return to the map x′ = γ(x − vt), t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), with its factor γ.
Return to finding the map that respects both light directions.

steps.text: Letters: the paper's stationary system K has coordinates x, y, z and time t; the moving system k has ξ, η, ζ and time τ, where τ is the time read on clocks at rest in k and set by §1's rule: a time coordinate, not a reading carried by one clock. V is the speed of light (c below), and the paper's β is the modern γ. The explanation writes \(x'\) and \(t'\) for ξ and τ. In §3 the paper also writes \(x'=x-vt\) for a different quantity, a Galilean helper coordinate, which is not ξ.

items: The shorter route this explanation takes first. k moves at speed v along K's x axis, and its origin follows x = vt. A point at rest in k keeps a fixed value of \(x-vt\), so the moving coordinate must be a multiple of it: \(x'=a(v)(x-vt)\), with a(v) not yet known.
The paper states why the map is linear: space and time are the same everywhere, so equal steps in one system correspond to equal steps in the other.
Write the time map as a general linear combination, \(t'=Pt+Qx\), and ask light to keep its speed c in k in both directions along x.
Light going right, x = ct: then \(x'=a(c-v)t\) and \(t'=(P+Qc)t\), and \(x'=ct'\) requires \(a(c-v)=c(P+Qc)\).
Light going left, x = −ct: then \(x'=-a(c+v)t\) and \(t'=(P-Qc)t\), and \(x'=-ct'\) requires \(a(c+v)=c(P-Qc)\).
Add the two conditions: \(2ac=2cP\), so P = a. Subtract them: \(-2av=2Qc^2\), so \(Q=-av/c^2\). That gives the time map below, with the same unknown factor.

steps.spoken: The light constraints give a common coefficient multiplying x minus vt and t minus vx over c squared.

items: Go to k and back. Transforming with speed v and then with −v must return every event unchanged. Put the first map into the second: \(x''=a(-v)a(v)\left[(x-vt)+v\left(t-\frac{vx}{c^2}\right)\right]=a(v)a(-v)\left(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)x\). So \(a(v)a(-v)(1-v^2/c^2)=1\).
Space has no preferred direction, so the factor cannot depend on which way k moves: a(v) = a(−v). Then \(a(v)^2=1/(1-v^2/c^2)\).
At v = 0 nothing changes, so a(0) = 1 and the positive root is the one. That root is γ, which is real only for speeds below c.

steps.spoken: The Lorentz factor is one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, giving the standard space and time transformation.

items: The paper's own route, which this explanation shortens. It writes \(x'=x-vt\), so that a point at rest in k has fixed \(x'\), y, z, and first finds τ as a function of \(x'\), y, z and t.

A light ray leaves the origin of k at τ₀, is reflected at \(x'\) at τ₁, and is back at τ₂; §1's rule in k requires \(\frac{1}{2}(\tau_0+\tau_2)=\tau_1\). In K the ray goes out at V − v and back at V + v, and taking \(x'\) very small turns the condition into a differential equation for τ: \(\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial x'}+\frac{v}{V^2-v^2}\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial t}=0\).

Light along the other two axes crosses, seen from K, at \(\sqrt{V^2-v^2}\), which gives \(\partial\tau/\partial y=0\) and \(\partial\tau/\partial z=0\). Since τ is linear, \(\tau=a\left(t-\frac{v}{V^2-v^2}x'\right)\).

A ray sent along ξ at τ = 0 has ξ = Vτ, and in K it moves away from k's origin at V − v, so \(x'/(V-v)=t\). Substituting gives \(ξ=a\frac{V^2}{V^2-v^2}x'\), and rays along the other axes give η and ζ. Putting back \(x'=x-vt\), the paper reaches \(τ=\varphi(v)\beta\left(t-\frac{v}{V^2}x\right)\), \(ξ=\varphi(v)\beta(x-vt)\), \(η=\varphi(v)y\), \(ζ=\varphi(v)z\), with \(\beta=1/\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\) and φ an unknown function of v.

The check that the two principles agree: a spherical light wave sent from the common origin at t = τ = 0, \(x^2+y^2+z^2=V^2t^2\) in K, becomes \(ξ^2+η^2+ζ^2=V^2\tau^2\) in k, a spherical wave of speed V there too.

Fixing φ: a third system moving at −v relative to k must be at rest relative to K, which gives \(\varphi(v)\varphi(-v)=1\). A rod along η, moving across its own length, has length \(l/\varphi(v)\) in K, and by symmetry that cannot depend on the direction of motion, so \(\varphi(v)=\varphi(-v)\). Together, φ(v) = 1, and the paper's printed result is \(τ=\beta(t-vx/V^2)\), \(ξ=\beta(x-vt)\), η = y, ζ = z.

margin.text: Einstein’s own §3 derivation follows a light signal out and back between clocks and solves a differential equation for the moving system’s time \(\tau\); the two-direction argument here is a shorter modern route to the same map. His \(\beta\) is the modern \(\gamma\), and his \(\tau\) is a coordinate time, not the proper time of modern texts.
